utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. And I think you indicated you'd needed another 15 minutes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour, and I'll endeavour to be as consistent with that as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we just for efficiency and to assist me in not going too far over the time I predicted, could we have 65 ter 06682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see here an article from Kozarski Vjesnik, 21 November 1993. Looking at the third column in the B/C/S in the centre and the bottom of page 1 in the English we read about the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May. We read: "After several hours of fighting, the attack was repulsed, the attackers routed and partly destroyed. In these actions several soldiers of the Serbian army and five policemen were killed." Just two quick questions about this. First, this is a reflection that the army did not go from Slavonia to Gradacac as you suggested yesterday at T40988, that it fought in Prijedor at the end of May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you allow me to say a couple of things. On the 30th May, when the attack happened, I was in my apartment all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer the question. If there's anything to be added, then at the very end of your testimony you have an opportunity to do so within certain limitations. But, at this moment, you should focus on answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the entire 43rd Brigade was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see here a reference to several hours of fighting. Does that refresh your recollection as to the length of the conflict on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An intervention group Karlica was stationed in Prijedor, and they were involved in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's an intervention group of the 43rd Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were on leave in Prijedor at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for me to clarify. You said they were on leave. Is it not being suggested to you that, in fact, they were the people fighting in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the attack on Prijedor, they, of their own initiative, engaged the attackers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 06682 receives exhibit number P7634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7634 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the army, meaning the VRS, also attacked Hambarine and Kozarac in late May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that that was also done by a couple of people on leave?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the former JNA. Some units were set up - I don't know which - but after the attacks on the reservists at Hambarine, they opened fire with some launchers or mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not clearly say what kind of launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you know, what kind of launchers, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And an ultimatum to hand over the people who'd done the attack on the reservists was issued by Commander Zeljaja; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that ultimatum. I know there was an ultimatum to all the paramilitary organisations to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer the question. The question was whether that ultimatum was issued by Commander Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33381, page 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is another portion of your Stakic testimony. Line 18, you're asked, "What did you hear about the shooting there," and from context it's the shooting you've just described on the reservists. "Who was shooting at whom? What was the demanding question? Can you explain -- can you give us more details?" You respond: "Oh I can just tell you what I heard from my neighbours. There was the killing of reservists at the check-point in Hambarine. I believe there were several wounded as well, and for a certain period of time the dead bodies were just lying there and access was denied to them. And later on, the army took over and dealt with the whole thing in military ...?" Turning to the next page: "... way so to say." And you were asked: "Do you know who was it who asked for the perpetrators for the weapons to be handed over? What did you hear? You responded: "I heard that it was the army who insisted on the surrender of the perpetrators. And they also said that nothing would happen. The ultimatum was rejected. I believe that at the time the commander was Zeljaja, the commander of the garrison. I believe his name was Radmilo Zeljaja." Do you stand behind the portions of your Stakic testimony that I've just read back to you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I couldn't confirm it or deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you said at the time or do you say, I ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was given by the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor together with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So does that mean that you stand by it or not? Because it was just read to you, what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you said the order was given by the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff, which order did you mean?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this proclamation was prepared for all local communes to collect all the weapons that had been distributed at that time. I was accidentally present in the Secretariat for the Economy when, from Cerik near Prijedor, people came bringing weapons. And at that time they reported to the secretary of the Secretariat for the Economy who had some role in this, and people from Kozarac came to say they are not going to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish quickly by returning to the graves. Now, you know the Tomasica, Redak and Jakarina Kosa grave-sites were all found on RZR Ljubija property; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You acknowledge it's possible that the VRS could have been involved in the burials at Tomasica; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33385, page 212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put the last question again to you but in a different form. Is there any reason for which you can exclude that the VRS could have been involved in those burials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no reason, either for or against, to exclude or to include.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did anyone from the 43rd Brigade every speak to you about mass graves on RZR Ljubija property?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did anyone from the military court ever speak to you about mass graves on RZR Ljubija property?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This talk was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "this talk," are you referring to the interview with staff of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal held last year?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So it's correct, then, that no one from the Banja Luka Military Court during the war ever spoke to you about mass graves on RZR Ljubija; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, last topic. A JOY drill is a drill that drills circular holes into rock; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In 1992, you knew precisely two of these machines existed as far as you knew in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Both of the drills that you knew of were owned by RZR Ljubija; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two and there were more. It's mining equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33390.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is the kind of hole a JOY drill creates, right, the circular hole in the rock we see here?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's identified as a picture from the Jakarina Kosa mass grave-site. You know about the exhumation there in 2001, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33399.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, you also know there have been additional exhumations as Jakarina Kosa this year; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you haven't heard that during the course of this year, as we see in the article on the screen, hundreds of human remains have been found during the re-exhumation of the Jakarina Kosa site in Prijedor this year?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow this. Believe me, I don't know. I know about funerals taking place at the cemetery not far from my own building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence, P3282, page 49, that the Jakarina Kosa site was under military control when it was created, that military explosives and other military equipment were found there. As the head of RZR Ljubija, you'd have to have known that the Jakarina Kosa site was under military control in the summer of 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that for some bodies, parts were found in the mass grave at Tomasica; parts were found of the same body in the Jakarina Kosa site. Now, you've testified just now that only two JOY machines you were specifically aware of in Prijedor municipality in 1993 were owned by RZR Ljubija. So these are people who had been buried at one spot on company property, dug up, reburied, to your knowledge probably with company equipment, at another spot on company property. Is it still your evidence that you somehow remained ignorant of this entire process?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- ask one question to the witness. Sir, I know that at the beginning of your testimony you told us about your career and how long you have been involved in the mining duties. Up to which moment have you been the director of the mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1991 to 1996 I was the general director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was there a reporting system in the mine about major and important events taking place under your authority and under your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't know if possibly an army unit or any other entity tried, either successfully or not successfully, to get control of parts of your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That enterprise at the time was not active. It was not producing anything. The director of the enterprise at Jakarina Kosa, the director of the unit at Jakarina Kosa, was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name. Who was the director of the unit at Jakarina Kosa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragoljub Kitonjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And please continue the sentence. What did you want to say about this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that he did not report to me about anything. He didn't inform me about anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And were you satisfied with this behaviour of this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was because the less I know, the more I'm worth in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said when it was put to you there were two drills. You said there were more. They were opened by the RZR Ljubija as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For different diameters of drilling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, I did not intervene when you earlier put to the witness that he said there were only two. The witness said there were more than the two, but apparently they were all owned by the same company. But would you please be very precise in putting to the witness what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd tender the last two documents, 65 ter 33390 and 33399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33390 receives exhibit number P7635.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33399 receives exhibit number P7636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'd requested imprecisely. There not being a translation yet, I should have clearly requested that it be MFI-ed pending the provision of one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's for the second one. And the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The first one was a photograph of the rock with the circular hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there was some title under it, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the top it says "Jakarina Kosa mass grave-site," I recall, and there's a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we can translate those few words if the Chamber deems it necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, or Mr. Stojanovic, any need to have that title over that first photograph to be sent for translation? It's on the transcript and it has been translated for the accused and everyone who speaks B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as we are concerned, Your Honours, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 65 ter number 33399 is marked for identification as P7636. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, when you said, sir, that you were satisfied that the head of the Jakarina Kosa area for RZR Ljubija didn't inform you of anything because the less you knew, the more you were worth, you say that because you didn't want to know what the military and police were doing with mobilised equipment on RZR Ljubija company property because you knew they were committing crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you say that I knew? You cannot say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honour. Could we please have P7385 in e-court. Could I please have page 3, both in B/C/S and in English. It is the last paragraph in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone is on, Mr. Stojanovic. When consulting, I would switch it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I would just like to say that it's pages 41029 and page 41027. That's where there was this dilemma regarding this document, Mr. Marjanovic. Again, I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph and the first sentence in the B/C/S version of the document. If you remember -- I'm going to ask you that you perhaps read out the first sentence once again, as you did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page in English, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's in the central part of the page that is before you. It is the seventh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Already in the beginning of the month of June, that is to say, only some ten days from when the fighting took place in time the complete direct security of buildings, property and persons was taken over from the military and police."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is the same sentence that we did a sight translation of yesterday and it is ambiguous in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters inform us that where the same sentence was read, that the original is ambiguous, though I do not know yet where exactly the ambiguity is, but -- and then there's another small matter. One second, please. Yes, it reads, and that what's I heard, "only some ten days from where the fighting took place in time," that's what was said, but I think it reads "in town," not "in time." Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And all that was not read by Judge Moloto but by the witness, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to try to resolve this definitely. When you read this document, when you look at it, Mr. Marjanovic, in this concrete case, who took over what from whom? That is to say, the security of buildings and property.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From whom did they take over?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security of the Ljubija mine took over the security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then from whom? Could you explain to us from whom they took over the security.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the army and police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then could you tell us when the army and the police had started their responsibility for security in the mine? Because if the Ljubija takes over again, then there must have been a moment when the army and the police had occupied or had ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 30th of May, after the attack at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When after? I mean, a week, two weeks, the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The 31st of May specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you explain to us why the army and the police on that day took over or at least were the ones who then secured the mine area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I assume that it was done for reasons of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whose security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security of buildings and people who worked in those plants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were not -- you were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that. I have already said, Mr. President, that during those five or six days I was at home because there was a curfew and people were not allowed to go out. What I said a moment ago is an assumption, that it's for the sake of the security and safety of the people who were there; also that they were trying to secure the property involved, the machinery, et cetera. That is what I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you haven't seen that happening yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give instructions that the mine -- the security of the company would take over again after ten days? Was it you who ordered that to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We had a security service within the mine and it was headed by Dusan Tubin who organised this part of the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't know about it or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, I did not know; but later on, I found out from him, 10 or 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask maybe the Prosecution about this document. Mr. Stojanovic asked the witness to tell us what this paragraph says and he says the Ljubija mine took over from the army and the police the responsibility for security. I don't see in the English paragraph even the name "Ljubija mine." And I know that the interpreters did say that the original is ambiguous, but it does seem as if not only is it ambiguous but the English is incomplete if, indeed, the B/C/S does refer to Ljubija mine, because on the English page, the entire page, I don't see Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: From the discussion, my response may be superfluous. But having been asked, I don't locate the words "Ljubija" in the relevant B/C/S paragraph either. I'd understood it that after it was read and sight-translated by the booth, Mr. Stojanovic had asked the witness to explain what it meant and the word came up in that context rather than appearing in the relevant B/C/S part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was not superfluous for me. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm relieved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to this document. Whose report is this, if you remember? Who is writing this report, this annual report, that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I do not remember who wrote this. I assume that it was Dusan Vlacina, my technical director.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that someone who is an employee of the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an employee, yes; but I'm not sure that he wrote it. He was the director there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to identify what it is that I'm saying, I would like to refer to the transcript from yesterday, page 41990, lines 17 through 20. Mr. Marjanovic, when you spoke about the cleansing of Prijedor, you mentioned the word "expropriation" in the old town. Could you please explain to us what this was actually about and what kind of process this is, this expropriation of that part of Prijedor, that area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area was populated by Muslims who had rather dilapidated houses. The Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor made a decision that they move out of that area. It is in the immediate vicinity of the Sana river and a part of it called Berak, and that a sports centre should be built there. For four or five years this went on, the expropriation of that area. That means that general interest had to be determined and then a deal should be struck with the owner of the immovable property involved. Most of these people, friends of mine, they got money and they built houses in the immediate vicinity, but practically the actual work involved for building the construction centre hadn't been started properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you referred us to yesterday's transcript, 41990, but I think that must be a misquote. Could you give the exact page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a moment, please. Page 40990, lines 17 through 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall end with a question that has to do with the question that was put to you today. Mr. Marjanovic, do you have any reason, any information or any indirect knowledge, to the effect that the Army of Republika Srpska was involved in any way in the burial of persons in Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, on behalf of the Defence of General Mladic, I would like to thank you for the effort that you have made in view of the condition of your health, and you stayed on today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have thus completed the examination of Witness Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before I give an opportunity for further questions to the Prosecution, again, you said, in answering the last question, that you have no reason, no information, no indirect knowledge to the effect that the Army of Republika Srpska was involved in any way. Now, do you have any knowledge, do you have any reason, do you have any information to the effect that they would not have been involved in it, or is it that you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that kind of knowledge either, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed -- Mr. Traldi, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, sir, Mr. Stojanovic asked you a moment about the cleansing of the Stari Grad neighbourhood. You referred to plans to build a centre there. Yesterday you'd called it a sports centre; today you referred to a construction centre. It's no accident and no coincidence that the demolition of those houses in that Muslim neighbourhood happened very shortly after the VRS attacked that neighbourhood, is it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, it is an accident; or yes, it is not?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, correction. I never said it was a construction building. I said it was a sports centre. And I did not say that these buildings were destroyed by accident after the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And today, at temporary transcript pages 15 and 16, you mentioned the head of the security service at RZR Ljubija, Dusan Tubin, and that he was who you claimed to have learned about the taking over of the responsibility for securing the company premises from. You agree, then, that he and not you would be the authoritative source on these issues; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. And I earlier said that if there was anything which you wished to further explain, that you have an opportunity at the end of your testimony. Is there any leftover now as part of an answer to the questions that were put to you that you'd like to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I wish to say that yesterday I was interrupted during my remarks by the Prosecutor. I tried to explain something then and that would have explained quite a bit and clarified quite a bit. The 43rd Brigade and the 5th Kozarska Brigade were the legal units in Prijedor. There were paramilitaries, at least 15 or 20 units. I can even give you some of the names. Almost every village had a unit of its own that appeared and tried to represent themselves as a unit, and their primary aim was to loot. That is what I wished to say then, and I was roughly interrupted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you were interrupted at the moment where you dwelled away from the question. But the 43rd brigade certainly was part of the questioning, so, therefore, does this trigger any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Very briefly, though I defer to Mr. Stojanovic if he has any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're the calling party. Anything you'd like to ask from the witness in relation to what he just told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question in relation to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Marjanovic, I've thanked you already but my apologies once again. Now, these paramilitaries, as you call them, how long did they operate in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, all the way up until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago every village had its own unit. That's how it was supposed to work under the Law on All People's Defence and the Territorial Defence system; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia that was the principle that existed. But this was a time of Yugoslavia's disintegration and there was a lack of authority and power and government of any kind. I don't want to go into any further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You weren't involved in the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was assigned to the air force of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you consequently have no personal knowledge of the 43rd Brigade's exercise of authority over Territorial Defence units in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge and my sources of knowledge are the workers from the Ljubija mines. Most of them were assigned to the 43rd Brigade, so it was in contact with them that I learned things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Now, we had a bit of an extended examination. I again repeat what I said before, that I thank you for coming, for having answered all the questions, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me just to greet all of those present in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no reason to do that, and certainly not if this is an indirect attempt, an indirect attempt to greet the accused. You may follow the usher, I said. You may leave this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant that I was supposed to -- I meant that I was supposed to say good-bye to everyone as I would leave. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, wouldn't it be wiser to take the break now and not to start for five minutes with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break now and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the next witness can be escorted in the courtroom. No protective measures. It would be Mr. Strbac, if we are well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strbac. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strbac. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already corrected me once with good morning. You said "good day," but English people say good morning until noon.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit different in our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please say for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: My name is Savo Strbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you live before the outbreak of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I was born in Dalmatia in a village called Rastivic in the Benkovac municipality. That's where I went to school. Then I continued in Benkovac, finished high schools, read law in Zagreb. I graduated from the law faculty in 1972. I returned from university to work in Benkovac in a few companies. At the same time, I clerked at the court. I believe it was in 1976 when I passed the bar and then I worked for a few years as a judge in the municipal court in Benkovac. And when I was appointed by Zagreb to the municipal court in Zadar, I worked there for a few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was a bit narrower. We have on the record that you worked in the municipal court in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It was the district court in Zadar, a higher level court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At what position did you work in that court?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I was a trial judge presiding over first-instance and appeals proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you organise an NGO?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I did. My NGO is called Veritas. It's full name is Veritas Documentation and Information Centre, and I established it together with a group of citizens from the then-Republic of Serbian Krajina towards the end of 1993. It still exists today, and I am still leading that organisation which now is based in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you decide to set up that NGO?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I've said before that I worked until October 1990 as a judge and already on the next day, on 1st November 1990, I started working as a lawyer. I had my own law practice. A few days before, I swore the lawyer's oath and became a member of the bar association of Croatia. I resigned by my own decision from the post in the district court in Zadar because it was obvious that some bad times were coming, and instead of presiding over normal criminal cases, they started bringing me heaps of cases against Serbs involving very petty things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason why you founded Veritas?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Not yet. At that time I became a lawyer, as I said, and in the same courtroom where I used to preside over large chambers, I started defending those Serbs that I was supposed to try. They were not all Serbs, to be frank. There were also some Croats who did not want to submit to the new regime. At that time I was confronted with many other problems. It was already obvious that there would be some kind of war and that there would be many dead on all sides. The writing on the wall was a civil war of which I had heard a lot from my elders from the Second World War. And in the meantime I read a book written --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to slow down a little, especially when you mention names and titles. Could you now please repeat the name of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Roadlessness of Historical Reality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also urge you to answer the questions because the question was why you founded the NGO. Now we know why you left the judiciary, what you then did, et cetera, but we still have no focussed answer on you founding the NGO. So could you please limit yourself to directly answering the question that is put to you. Please proceed, and now I would be pleased if it would be an answer, a direct answer, to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to say that. In that book by Franjo Tudjman, I encountered one piece of information that in the concentration camp of Jasenovac in the Second World War, 30 to 35.000 people were killed, and I was taught at all levels of education that 700.000 people were killed in fact. And when you are confronting a very new situation that smells of war and even after the war began, because I founded my organisation in 1993, then I said to myself now with my collaborators I will start to gather evidence, contemporaneous evidence, about the suffering of my people. That was the most immediate reason to found a non-governmental organisation because, at that time, in 1993 I was living in an unrecognised state called the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and my friends from around the world who were touring theatres of war on all the three sides suggested to me, in a way, that nobody opens the mail of an unrecognised state and that's why I should start an NGO, and through that NGO, spread information about the suffering of my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did Veritas collaborate with?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: With all international organisations, in fact, all those who were involved with human rights and war crimes and which had offices in the Serbian Krajina or the former Yugoslavia, including the ICTY; that is to say, the ICRC; UNPROFOR when they were present with the civilian and military components; the OSCE, the monitoring mission of the European Community; the International Commission for Missing Persons; and domestic organisations from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Croatia who were investigating war crimes and involved with human rights, because already from July 1991, I conducted the first exchange of prisoners between Serbia and Croatia, and since then, I've been involved with exchanges, prosecutions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm making a pause to give a breather to the interpreters. I would like to go back to 1990 now and the establishment of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. Do you remember when the HDZ was established?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, in the public eye, it was in February 1990 with a very pompous founding assembly in the largest hall in Zagreb called Lisinski. Of course, I remember it. The Croats remember it well but I believe the Serbs remember it even better in Croatia because at that founding assembly we saw something that we thought we'd never see again; that is to say, all the iconography of the Croatian Ustasha from the Second World War, the same coats of arms, the same symbols, the same songs. People who had run away from Yugoslavia, run away from the law, and found shelter abroad had returned, and this sent cold shivers down our spines and chilled our blood, I mean the Serbs. Later I thought a lot about that problem and found out that, in fact, the HDZ was established a year earlier in secret, in a shed in some obscure place. I remember well what it looked like on the ground because I worked in Zadar --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they chose the military option and started preparing?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: All of us who lived in those times, like me, in that area found out early on. In the beginning of 1990, when in every village, every hamlet, HDZ boards were being set up, they had already started wearing uniforms and arming themselves. From the court building, I had the opportunity to see the distribution of arms through the window because we shared that courtyard with the Zadar police, and then we, judges and prosecutors and clerks, would come out to watch. It was an old building like this one, maybe even older. The third, fourth floor, we were rather high up. We got out of the building to see exactly what was going on, so you see some perfectly new people, new uniforms, whole boxes of weapons being distributed, and later I found out it was going on all throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm addressing both you, Mr. Strbac, and you,

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simple questions are put to you. You give lengthy answers with, to some extent, highly irrelevant information. Whether you saw something happening from the third floor or the fourth floor and whether it was an old building or a new building isn't really the gist of what Mr. Lukic, I think, wants to elicit as evidence from you. So could I urge you not to deliver long speeches, all perhaps very interesting information, but Mr. Lukic is limited in his time. He puts questions to you and I take it that he would like to have answers. If you take so much time, at the end, Mr. Lukic may run out of time and not receive answers to questions remaining. So I am seeking your co-operation in limiting yourself to what is asked. And, Mr. Lukic, it's for you also to keep tighter control over what happens, because simple questions, one full page of answer with, again, sometimes an answer to your question; sometimes even not. Could I urge you to assist this Court in doing its job. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We lawyers and university professors are usually too verbose so I would kindly ask you to shorten your answers a bit. The Court received information here about the HDZ winning the election in Croatia so I'm not going to dwell on that. This is what I'd like to ask you now: After the victory in the elections, what did the HDZ do? What did they do first?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, there are no simple questions. I cannot just give a yes or no answer to this question. Purges started in the police, in all companies. In the police, they thought there were too many Serbs so then they were being laid off. I mean, I defended them so I know how many were laid off. Then in companies, likewise, there were too many Serbs. For example, in the fire brigade in Zadar, all the Serbs were laid off because somebody said if there was a fire, the Serbs won't want to extinguish it, and so on and so forth. On the approaches leading to industrial towns where people from the neighbouring villages worked, people were thrown out of buses, sent back home on foot, and then they would be laid off after five days because the legal requirement was to call in at work, and if you would not appear for five days, then you would be laid off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, just to help you, the simple answer therefore would have been: The HDZ started purging the police, companies, and other institutions from Serbs. That's the short answer. If Mr. Lukic is interested to know whether it was done by throwing people out of buses or in any other way, or whether the five days, he'll ask you. So let's try to keep matters as simple as possible, even if it's not a yes or no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were insignia on uniforms changed and official emblems on institutions?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of insignia were used then?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Instead of the five-pointed star that was the emblem for the military and the police, the police used the chess-board first, the one from the Second World War at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the chess-board emblem linked to?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The Ustasha movement for the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did Serbs react? For example, policemen.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, the Zadar policemen, Croats and Serbs, wrote a petition to the federal authorities. They sought protection from such insignia and emblems and they were warning that new policemen were being admitted into the force, people with criminal records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to those policemen who were warning about these things that were happening, that is to say, having criminals brought into the police?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Disciplinary proceedings were instituted against them and often they would result in these people getting laid off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I defended them the most, and there were a few more lawyers. However, I had a leading role because I had a great deal of experience as a criminal lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many cases of this kind did you have?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Certainly more than a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened in respect of the position of the Serbs according to the constitution? Was the constitution changed? Just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of December, 1990, the Croatian Parliament promulgated a Christmas constitution, and the Serbs were no longer a constituent people. They became a national minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did Serbs react to that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Along parallel lines, just as Croats were making decisions about separation from the SFRY, Serbs in Croatia made decisions to separate from Croatia and they established, first of all, the SAO Krajina and then there were these three SAO Krajinas. These are Serb independent regions. And then in December, they all became part of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. They united to become that republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time in official circles in Croatia, was there an anti-Serb campaign?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Everything was an anti-Serb campaign, at least that's how we felt, and I believe that everything was directed against Serbs. And it was. You know, when the head of state, the president, greets Croat men and women to congratulate them on the Christmas holidays and when he says that he is happy that his wife is not a Jew or a Serb, that is something that Serbs would not welcome. On the contrary. They would become fearful. And my professor from university who later became a minister, the minister of defence, he said that Serbs had heads that were much smaller than Croat heads and that they were of a different shape, and so on. And it's not just anybody who is saying this. This is a university professor who later became a minister.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are again invited to slow down. And perhaps, again, your first answers after I asked you to focus were really meeting my request. The later answers, less, however. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that your natural way of responding is one of eloquence, an extended manner, if you will, but as the Judge told you we don't have all that time. So please give the briefest answer as possible and at the same time speak more slowly. In your view, this is what you said to us: At how many levels did this anti-Serb campaign exist?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I quoted Jovan Raskovic who divided this into three levels: The everyday level, or the aggression of the consciousness. That was in the street, at work, different pressures. Then there was the administrative level. That was in companies, in socio-political organisations, in the army, the police, et cetera, for example, those layoffs. And the political level, that is, the minimizing of Serb rights, like representing the population numbers as lower, and then that led to a decrease in political rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are still in 1990. I'll go back. You started telling us about how you started your own law practice and how you left the court, and you explained to us why you decided to take that step. You said that you represented policemen. Just tell us what kind of proceedings were these, the policemen who were laid off?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, these were disciplinary proceedings. In the police, there were disciplinary courts. They were rather well-organised. And then also before regular courts in criminal cases, misdemeanour cases, civil cases, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us talk about ordinary companies for a while. Were there companies that laid off people?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of them, they did that straight away. And I can give examples all day long. But let's say now I remember the shoe factory in Gradacac, its name was Simecki, and their head office was in Zagreb. 550 employees did not receive salaries for months and ultimately they were laid off. My office and I filed 550 complaints asking for compensation. Of course, we did not win a single case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you again move away from the questions. The question was about companies that laid off people. Now you said almost all of them did. You gave an example. And then you started telling us about proceedings which was not part of the question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would be my next question. However, since you've already answered my question, I think that the name of the place that you referred to was misrecorded.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: This is obviously somebody from Bosnia. Somebody wrote Gradacac but this is Gracac, in Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no reason to in any way make your suggestions or what caused mistakes and whether that is the background of those who are either transcribing or interpreting for us. Would you refrain from such comments. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about these layoffs after five days. In order to explain this to us, could you explain the ethnic composition of the population in terms of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: For example, Lika and Dalmatia, where I lived the most and I'm most familiar with that area, for the most part, this industry was concentrated in locations that were outside the Republic of the Serb Krajina, that is to say, outside the areas where Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Serbs went to work by travelling?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Every day. Taking buses to Split, Sibenik, Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at one moment, what happened? What did the Croatian side --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I've already said. On the approaches to towns, there were some kind of armies, police forces, armed with these new emblems of Croatia, with the chess-board emblems. And then they would get them off buses and send them back to their villages, their homes, on foot. They would do that for five days, and then on the fifth day they would get laid off because, according to the law, whoever did not appear at work for five days would be laid off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you travel to work in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I had Zadar licence plates. I used my own car. I went through barricades every day. And once the registration of my car expired, then I travelled by bus; but then at the end of August 1991, the buses weren't running any longer either, so then I just couldn't go anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you go through barricades? How come they allowed you to do that at all?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I had an ID of the Croatian bar. And before that, I would agree with the police before I would travel. Then they would give orders to these people at these posts that were basically machine-gun nests to let me go through, and then they would let me go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People, ordinary people, did they mind these restrictions on movement? Were there cases when somebody would leave and then not return?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Barricades were there for already one year but people could still not accept that. People went to the seaside, to places where they had gone for years. So a person would go to take a swim in the sea and would get arrested. And then I went there to defend such persons and get them out of jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did Serbs react to arrests of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: In one specific case when Croats arrested five persons who went to the seaside to take a swim, then my people, that is to say, in Benkovac, arrested eight Croats. And then they asked for an exchange and then I handled that exchange. It was my first exchange, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us how you organised this exchange. Through whom?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I was given power of attorney from the families of the arrested Serbs and I defended them. We were supposed to have a court hearing, and I suggested to the investigative judge who was my colleague because we were judges together in that very same court, well, I said, "Let's see." I mean, nobody's guilty there, and I asked him to suggest to the Croatian police to release the arrested Serbs and I would tell the people in Benkovac to release the arrested Croats. They agreed to that after consultations with Zagreb and then there was an exchange on the border between the municipalities of Benkovac and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask you something about the illegal import of weapons. Was there any illegal import of weapons into Croatia and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I've already said that I looked in the courtyard of the Zadar court how weapons were distributed from trucks that had entered the courtyard. There was arms distribution all over the place. Later on, we found out from where these weapons were imported. Now everyone knows it all. First of all, weapons were imported from Hungary. The army filmed a documentary about it, and I first watched it in January 1991 but it was filmed in the October of the previous year, 1990. In that documentary, in that film, you can see the protagonists of that movie, such as Mr. Spegelj, who later became a minister of defence in the government, talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When this illegal import of weapons was discovered, what did the Croatian authorities do?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: In the beginning, weapons were distributed to members of the HDZ along party lines. At that time, Croatia was still a Yugoslav republic, so federal authorities took the decision on disarming throughout the SFRY, disarming of all paramilitary units. Croatians asked for 48 hours' grace, and during those 48 hours, they convert all these paramilitaries into members of the police so that the police force increased within a few days to 71.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many did they have before?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the weapons in Serbian police stations, in areas where Serbs were the majority in settlements and in police stations?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It was on 17 August 1990 that the Croatian police set out into Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, Korenica, Knin, and other Serb majority areas, to disarm these police stations. The police also had its reserve force and reserve police weapons were kept in the depots attached to police stations. They managed to do that in Benkovac. It was in the small hours after midnight. Then people from Benkovac warned the others. And that's when the log revolution, as it is known, started. The Serbs rebelled. They set up logs on the road, or rocks, as roadblocks to prevent further incursions into their police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move briefly to 1991 to see the development of interethnic relations in 1991. Let's say the beginning of May in Zadar. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: "The Glass Night," we all know where that name comes from, 1938 in Germany. Something similar happened in May 1991 in Zadar when people started flowing into the city in buses, in an organised way, and unmistakably attacked all Serbian businesses or offices of Serbia-based companies damaging or destroying them. There was a lot of glass shattered everywhere so it was called The Glass Night, although it happened during day-time. If you allow me to add, on the same day at the other end of Croatia, in the east --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my next question. What happened at the other end of Croatia on the same day?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Borovo Selo, the Borovo village, populated by Serbs, a delegation from Croatia was supposed to come for peace talks on that day, but instead of coming in peace, the Croats came in with a full busload of MUP officers who started shooting at Serb houses, and the Serbs returned fire. There were people dead and wounded and captured, and many theoreticians consider that to be the beginning of the conflict in Croatia, although there was an incident earlier on that I considered to be the beginning and that was 31st March of the same year at Plitvice, which is the Plitvice case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are talking about Plitvice, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Plitvice were at that time kept by members of the Territorial Defence from Serbia. Plitvice Lakes are a famous tourist spot. And Croatian policemen arrived as tourists at a hotel. They had their weapons concealed and disassembled in suitcases. They assembled these weapons and launched an attack. One Serb policeman and one Croatian policeman were killed in the incident. Goran Hadzic was captured, taken prisoner on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me return to your own region, something that you were involved in. First of all, do you know who is Dragisa Vranjes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is special about his fate?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: He is a Serb born in Cetina village, Knin municipality, and he was working in Switzerland. Sometime in July 1991 he was travelling from Switzerland to Belgrade and then on to Croatia by bus. They took him off the bus somewhere on the way to Zagreb, near Zupanje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you again please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] And that's where all trace of him goes cold. We know he set out from Belgrade and then nothing. Around 15 August, there was an exchange of prisoners between Knin and Sibenik and one of the prisoners says that he is sure that Dragisa was in the Sibenik prison because he had a very deep voice. He was a very large man and had a bass voice. This man heard Dragisa being tortured and beaten and screaming and moaning. They paraded him around town as a Chetnik from Cetina. So Dragisa, after all that torture, fell silent one night. Since we were dealing with that case, one lawyer friend of mine and I, we wanted to find out from anyone who might know, including his family, whether he had actually ended up in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you remember the name of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Radomir Kuzet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how did you get involved in this?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: At the request of the family and Milan Martic and Jovan Raskovic and Milan Babic and everyone who meant something in Krajina, we were asked to find out what happened to that man. It's a very long story. In any case, we were told by the chief of police that he had died from a heart stroke on the 24th in a hospital and that he was buried at an out-of-the-way cemetery. And in our presence the body was exhumed. We transported it to Knin. And after the post-mortem, it was impossible to transport the body to his village because the road was blocked on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. So, first of all, where was the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Kijevo village. It's a Croatian place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who blocked the road?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The Croat police. In Kijevo, as in many other places, the Croat police established new police stations with the chequer-board symbol, and they blocked the road. You couldn't use it. You couldn't reach the other villages. And as far as I know, and today it's accepted knowledge among historians, the JNA set out to lift that blockade. There was shooting from both sides. There were people wounded and arrested and taken prisoner. I don't know if any were killed. But that was in the early days. That was the beginning of the JNA's turning against the Croats. There were 18 such police stations in different places that had never had a police station before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did policemen react to the request that Dragisa Vranjes passed through Kijevo to be buried in Cetina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: They were unable to go on. They had to turn back. They were supposed to take him from Civljane to Cetina. These are neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in any way after Dragisa Vranjes' body was taken to Knin? Did you participate in further negotiations or did your role end there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: You mean only Dragisa and his case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, we had finished with him. We turned over the body to his family. But it's interesting that he was not in a casket. He was just wrapped in a sheet. And his family was unhappy. And as soon as his body was taken out of the car, the family attacked us lawyers because the body in the sheet weighed only 60 kilos, whereas the man, while he was alive, weighed 120 kilos. Anyway, it was summer. The earth was dry. He had been buried before, and the soil simply melted all his fat. There remained only skin and bones. That's perhaps a curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said this was the moment when the JNA turned against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Not only that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Take it easy. I'll put my questions. That was the beginning of the conflict; right? Did there come a time when JNA barracks were blocked?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: There was an appeal already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Very simple. If we can have a date when this was happening, the JNA against Croats in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a suggestion that you'd seek --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's in the transcript, but that's what witness said but I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This incident in Kijevo village, the conflict surrounding the passage of Dragisa Vranjes's body --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was on the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's return to the blockade of JNA barracks. When was that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked not to start answering when -- and it's too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you, when I put my question, to wait a little before answering, to make a pause between question and answer. That's my mistake. I should have told you this at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And wait for a question to be there, to start with. So don't answer if there's no question yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your memory, when did the blockade of JNA barracks begin?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It began already in 1991 with the arming drives, when the party soldiers were converted into police officers. It was still the army, the federal army, and federal laws prohibited different armies. So the Croats had the clever idea of making it police force, not an army. JNA soldiers received appeals to leave their barracks. Croat soldiers, indeed, left, but Serb soldiers and other ethnicities remained in the barracks, remained in the army, the federal army. And I remember, I think it was on the 5th of May when the president of Croatia, Tudjman, at an assembly in Trogir, made a public appeal to start attacking the JNA. And after that appeal, there was this notorious incident in Split when a soldier of the JNA, a Macedonian boy, was strangled atop his APC and an all-out attack started in mid-September, 15 September. Throughout Croatia barracks were blocked. JNA troops were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. We started a bit early. Usually, I ask the witness to follow the usher before I make any comments, but you've used now almost an hour, and we'll be rather strict in time because much of the questions are background rather than related to what seems to be the core of the case. And apart from that, even if it's background, and you know that the Chamber never has prevented the Defence from also presenting background information, although foreground is first to focus at, but then we lose ourselves in quite many details, which really do not assist the Chamber in any way. So, therefore - and I'm saying this in the presence of the witness who, from his professional background, should know that as well - if you want your testimony to be effective in this courtroom, try to focus on the questions. And you, Mr. Lukic, if there's anything on the foreground we should know, give that priority at this moment so that we get a fair balance between what is background and what is information related to the core of this case. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, the behaviour I noticed when I entered this courtroom is totally inappropriate. You should refrain from dealing with the public gallery in the way you did. Let that be clear. And it's the last warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed. And please keep in mind what I said before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about people who were being laid off. Were there people from Bosnia among them?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. So they did not treat them on the basis of republic affiliation but ethnic affiliation. As far as I know, many people from Bosnia worked in Croatia because there were a lot of industrial facilities. For example, I know that many of them worked at the steelworks in Sisak at the refinery, and if they were ethnic Serbs, they were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, would they remain in Croatia or would they leave; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: They would leave. They would go back to their place of birth, if they had someone there. What also happened was that these people who were born in Bosnia would be gathered together and then taken further down south to some islands and then they would return them to Bosnia from there. Unfortunately, some of them lost their lives on their way back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about blockades of JNA barracks in Croatia. Did you know General Mladic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to remember now. Yes, yes. Several times. Yes, I saw him several times. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to all of that. First I'd like to ask you about the Bjelovar barracks now. What do you know about the fate of the barracks there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: On the 29th of September, as far as I remember, after a blockade of the barracks that went on for several days, the barracks surrendered. The officers lined up all the troops, and they surrendered. They realised that they could not put up a resistance any longer. Upon entering the barracks, some Ure Simic, who was head of Crisis Staff, ordered that these three main officers be executed. According to my information, he executed them himself. He fired two bullets at each and every one of them. As a matter of fact, there are criminal proceedings currently underway against him in Croatia, precisely because of that murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the warehouse in Bedenik?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I think it was about 15 kilometres away from the barracks in town, and that's where an officer, Tepic, didn't want to hand over this warehouse to the Croatian army or police. He mined it and blew it up. People say that there were 170 tonnes of explosive there, and, of course, he blew himself up too and with him was a soldier of his who didn't want to obey him and who didn't want to leave him, who stayed there with him. The other casualties involved were about 11 Croat soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that two officers were killed --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Three. Three officers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot follow because the two speakers are speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you should make a pause between question and answer, and between answer and question. All the other matters I raised before are still valid as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. I should have paused. Could you please tell us what happened with the other soldiers from the Bjelovar barracks, except for these three who were executed.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
