utterances.text: Six of them -- actually, six local people who, as far as I know, were civilians who were working in the army, they were taken away to the police station in town, and after four or five days, they were taken out and executed. As for the rest, the soldiers who were doing their regular military service, and there was some NCOs there as well and there were more than 250 of all of them, they were taken to some sports halls. That's where screening took place, triage. Young soldiers were allowed to go home. As for the rest, depending on ethnicity, they were either arrested and then exchanged later or taken to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about the position of the JNA but now we're going to discuss the position of civilians in 1991. For example, could you tell us what happened to Serbs in Gospic? Where is Gospic in relation to the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: In Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Lika. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Gospic is in Lika. I had a law office in Lika, in Korenica. And my wife is from Lika so I'm familiar with the area, just as I'm familiar with Dalmatia. Serbs in Gospic fell victim in 1991. According to the data collected by my organisation, it is 124 victims. So I'm talking about civilians. An investigation took place before the Prosecutor's office of The Hague Tribunal. However, before issuing the indictment, the whole case was referred to Croatia. Croatia tried five people and three were found guilty of these crimes and convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These Serbs who were killed in Gospic, is that the general population? Had some people left? Could you please tell us more about this.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Most people stayed. How do we put this? These were loyal citizens of the newly established authorities. And some of them even carried weapons. There was civilian protection there. They guarded bridges, for instance, and so on. Unfortunately, they were killed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slavonska Pozega, what do you know about that? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Slavonska Pozega, an order was issued there as well, also at the end of October. I think it was the 29th again, but October, not September. And it was the Crisis Staff of Pozega, so it's Croats, they issued a written order to evacuate 26 villages that had a Serb population predominantly or exclusively. They pretended that the population could return but they just wanted to cleanse the area of enemies, Chetniks. The people never went back. As soon as they left, their houses were torched, their property was looted, and the few old people who stayed behind were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people who moved from their homes, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Through Bosnia. Some people stayed in Bosnia, and some -- most of them went to Serbia. And after that, they went all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us something else. We said the 29th of October. What's the year?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: 1991. We're still talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to Serbs in Bilogora?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The same. Two days later, the 31st of October, the Croats carried out some operation that they called Otkos-10 and then I think they mowed down about 26 villages, according to the same principle, like before in the Pozega valley. People would be expelled. Their homes and properties would be looted, and people had no place to go, to return. If somebody stayed on, then they would get killed. Again, we're talking about over 60 victims. And as for the previous case, it involves 70 victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in exchanges of people who were taken prisoner in these areas?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, but only from 1993 onwards, so it wasn't at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about camps for Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Already in the Autumn of 1991, the most notorious camps were in Western Slavonia, Pakracka Poljana and Ribarska Koliba, or Marino Selo. Those are the names of the camps. They're right next to one another. According to the information collected by Veritas, over 300 persons went through these camps. Most of them are still missing. Currently, a Croat, Tomislav Mercep, is being tried for crimes in these camps. The proceedings are taking place before a Croatian court. In addition to that camp, there were camps that Croats called places where detainees could stay, and that would suggest a motel or a hotel and it is actually camps like Lora and Kerestinec that were behind that misnomer. People were tortured like during the times of the Inquisition in the Middle Ages. Before Croatian courts, there are proceedings for both Lora and Kerestinec. There are already three cases concerning Lora. One has been completed; there's a final judgement of conviction. One is under way right now, the trial is underway. And the third one is still in the investigation stage. As for Kerestinec, there was also a conviction. However, it has been quashed and there is a retrial now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go to General Mladic now. When did you first meet General Mladic; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. Sometime in October, Mladic's men from Knin came, because he was commander of the Knin Corps at the time, they came to see me in Benkovac. And since I was a reserve officer, they brought me call-up papers and they said that they are appointing me some president of some court, and that already on the following day, I should organise a trial for some deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you: Which year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991. All of this is 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I also? Can you then answer the question that was put to you: When did you first meet Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, right now. Right now. Now I've been telling you about how I went to the command in Knin where the command post is and where Mladic was and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question that was put to you. The question put to you is when did you meet Mr. Mladic. That's what I'm asking you to please answer. What the Presiding Judge has been telling you all this morning, to please focus on the questions an answer the question and not tell a story. The answer to the question must tell us time or date. "I met Mr. Mladic on such and such a date."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I give you an answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall the date. It was October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the name of this man who came to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Hasotic is his last name. Yes. Mesud Hasotic. He was assistant commander for morale, so he was Mladic's assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you know what his ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. He's a Muslim at the time, yes, and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to be tried?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Serbs, some Serbs there who fled from the positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the trial happen?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Fortunately, it didn't, because I didn't know under what legislation I was supposed to try them. They returned to their positions and there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that court established?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Never. If you mean military court or court-martial, such a thing was never established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since that trial never happened, what were you told about your duties?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: First I went to Banja Luka where there were many eminent lawyers, to talk to them, to see if there was a possibility to create some legislation, courts for me to test my knowledge and experience, and we concluded together it was not possible to organise any trials except before the regular courts that already existed in the SFRY system. And the next day, Hasotic told me, "Go home. You are the most useful and the best when you are working on your own on these exchanges," because I was the only connection between Krajina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go with General Mladic for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I think it was already in December 1991 when one exchange with Croats from Gospic was blocked. We had reliable information that in their prison, under a special regimen, there were some members of the JNA who had been taken prisoner in the barracks in Gospic, and they would not reveal them, either to us or to the ICRC. Then Mladic came as reenforcement on our team and we dealt with that problem successfully. The Croats, upon seeing Mladic, and because he was very delicate and wise in his conduct with them, confessed that they were holding some JNA officers under special regimen, and in the period that followed we organised that exchange. I think one of the officer's names is Dusko Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else, any other officer, accompany you at these exchanges when Mladic was not there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Hasotic, as the assistant commander for morale, I suppose it was part of his job description. Sometimes Tolimir went. He was also one of Mladic's assistants in Knin, and I think he was a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who headed the Croatian delegation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: In this specific case, the Croats from Gospic were headed by a certain Dr. Jerkovic, who was president of the Crisis Staff. Yes, Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did he introduce his delegation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: On our delegation, we had a man from Gospic, Slobodan Pogramilovic, and he noticed that the boss, Jerkovic, gave all the others some different names. So we passed a note to Mladic, and I think it was thanks to that that Mladic at one point addressed people by their real names and then they were disarmed, so to say, and they admitted to something they had had no intention of admitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it then that it was revealed Dusko Bajic was held by them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness, again, is starting to answer before the question is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you started answering before the interpretation of the question was finished. The question was: Was it then that it was revealed Dusko Bajic was held by them? Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was. It was then that it was revealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Croats bring arrested Serb civilians to these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs bring Croat civilians to exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Both sides held some civilians. However, on the Croat side, in that year, 1991, people were rounded up in the street and arrested in their apartments just for the purpose of exchanges, not that they were arrested because of some misdemeanour. They just didn't have enough people for exchanges so they would round up people in the streets and in their apartments and bring them to the exchange. That was a very frequent occurrence in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there cases where one civilian was exchanged more than once?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. In Zadar, for instance, I remember a man called Pavle Opsenica, a JNA officer who was retired just before the war broke out. He had a Croat wife and children and an apartment in Zadar. They brought him for an exchange twice. He would be brought to Knin and both times he returned to his family. The third time they came to pick him up, but he wasn't taken to an exchange but towards Zagreb. It is known that he had reached Mount Velebit and then he went missing. Nobody knows what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have one more topic outstanding and then we'll probably conclude before the time we had announced. Knowing about your volubility, I allowed for some extra time. We'll be discussing UNPROFOR now. In your view, what was the role of UNPROFOR in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: As for the role that was intended for them, that's written in the UN Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm really struggling to understand what is the relevance of this topic to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a question about relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw many reports written by UNPROFOR. We should understand their acts and conducts in the field, what was its role. It's not only what was written on the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the Krajina, in that period of time? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Krajina, and we also dealt with the same topic in Bosnia. I think we dealt in -- for Bosnia in a lengthy manner, challenging their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time-frame and that period -- time-frame and that location, what does it add? What is the relevance for us? I mean, of course we want to understand whatever happened in the world over the last 20 centuries, but the question is whether it assists us in doing our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Time-frame should be 1992 to 1995. Sorry, Your Honour. I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought we are now talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1991. By now I changed the topic, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your next questions, please keep them focussed, not "what is your understanding of this or that" because that's opinion you're asking for. Be focussed and ask for factual knowledge of this witness, because the witness has presented to us already many, many facts where he apparently has not been a witness himself. I didn't stop you there or didn't stop the witness there. I take it that most likely, although it is unclear, it's on the basis of his documentation. But let's try to focus and treat him as a witness of fact - that's how he was introduced - and then on relevant matters. Keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strbac, how much of your life did you dedicate to the study of the events in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: All this time, since I started my law practice, that is to say, 1st November, 1990, I never stopped. And throughout the war, I co-operated with all the international organisations that were represented in Krajina, and I know all about it, the UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the Europe Community Monitoring Mission. All this is my immediate knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, it's not an answer to the question anymore because it was how long did you work on it. Second, you gave that answer already to a previous question which Mr. Lukic asked you, that is, with whom you co-operated. I really have to insist that it's focussed, that it's factual, and that it is relevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I asked you in your view, what was the role of the UNPROFOR? How did it affect the status of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? And I'll later ask you about specific actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interfered last time mainly because you were asking for opinion. That's what you're doing now as well. So could you please proceed, Mr. Lukic, with questions of fact that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the Nos Kalik operation; do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I do. It was on the 2nd of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: At that time, UNPROFOR forces were still in the process of being deployed in Krajina. The Croats took advantage of that moment, and they launched a first operation against the Serb village, Oskanik [phoen]. And there was Territorial Defence and army involved. About 20 residents were arrested. They were later exchanged, but they had been badly beaten in prisons before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up to June 1992, was UNPROFOR already deployed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. They deployed according to that leopard-skin system, or ink stains, as we say, across the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the Miljevacki Plateau operation, and what was the role of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: It was another Croat operation against one part of the Krajina. It was on the 21st of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are talking about June 1992. General Mladic is in Bosnia. We are talking about Croatia. I still don't understand why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Acts and conducts of UNPROFOR, that's what we are talking about, the same UNPROFOR. The seat of UNPROFOR in Bosnia is in Zagreb, Croatia. That is their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, but that doesn't mean that everyone who was there, the acts and conduct of those persons, companies, entities, whatever, becomes relevant. I mean, it's not that if you are at the same time more or less in the same geographical area, that that makes it all relevant. Could you please focus your question on matters which are clearly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm focussing on the questions that are clearly relevant for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then tell me what the relevance is, apart from that they were there at the same time in the same area. That may be true for all kinds of things or persons or groups or whatever. Focus on what they did, what the witness personally knows about it, and then that, by putting the questions, that it is clear to us that it's relevant. Otherwise, we'll have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, what was your knowledge, what was your information, about how UNPROFOR acted in that situation? Were they supposed to protect the Serbs, the Serb residents there? What did they actually do?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: We Serbs were expecting UNPROFOR to protect us, and that's why we sort of relaxed. However, they did not protect us. They said it was not their role. It was not their mandate to protect anyone using weapons, and all they could do on the ground - and that's how they behaved - was to write reports and send them to their headquarters. And then the Security Council adopted certain resolutions which again were not observed on the ground. In this specific case, on the Miljevacki Plateau, 43 members of the Territorial Defence were killed. Some were killed even after being taken prisoner. And UNPROFOR's sole help to us was in taking them out of the pit into which they had been thrown two months later. They were so mutilated, these bodies, that 12 have still not been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that the witness is referring to his documentation. We don't know anything about that. Again, he is more or less appearing now and your questioning him as if he were an expert on cultural or historical background. He is introduced as a witness of fact. I also now understand that the gist of what you want to elicit - but correct me if I'm wrong - is that UNPROFOR at the time did not intervene to protect the Serbs. I don't know whether there's any dispute about that, first of all, that they did not intervene at these occasions. If there's no dispute, then try to seek agreement on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see if the Prosecution does not dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? No, not let's see. You should have inquired. It is the task of the parties to seek contact with the other party to see whether there's any dispute about matters of fact. I wouldn't expect Mr. Zec now to immediately know this, but that's your task which you should have performed before. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Through my questions, and ask the Prosecution if they agree with me before direct examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, look at the rules. You should have done this even before the start of the trial. Parties should try to agree, to the extent possible, on what is in dispute and what is not. Don't tell me now that this is a task that only falls upon you in court. That's just ignoring what the rules are telling you and it's ignoring what we have said a lot of times. I don't know whether Mr. Zec would agree that UNPROFOR has, in these attacks, not intervened. I leave it apart from why not or whether they could not or whether they did, but whether they did not intervene in such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It all depends on specific situations. In general, we can agree that sometimes UN was unnatural in attacks, but we would know -- need to know a little bit more what Mr. Lukic is referring to, what operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if that would have been discussed before, we would have saved a lot of time. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have another -- you said you would take less time but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Quarter past 1.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have approximately until a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll finish by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Medak pocket operation, when did it take place, and was it likely for the role of UNPROFOR to be changed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Operation Medak Pocket, did it seem that things would change after that in terms of how UNPROFOR acted, how they acted in cease-fires, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: May I? May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, you are on your feet, then you're down again, on your feet. Do you want to object, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, the same objection, Your Honours. We are well above 1991 and I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I'm not going to stop Mr. Lukic, although I urged him several times to examine the witness in such a way that it would assist the Chamber. The Chamber is also not inclined to spend the next 15 or 20 minutes on discussing what is relevant and what is not relevant. Mr. Lukic knows, I think, meanwhile what would assist us and what would not. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us whether in 1993 you had a role in the exchange of prisoners? Tell us about the period after the Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I listened to the discussion. I'm speaking on the basis of my very own experience because I took part in all these actions as president of the commission for the exchange of the dead and prisoners of Republika Srpska Krajina. So it's my very personal knowledge, not only through my organisation, Veritas. The Medak pocket occurred in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us the year.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: 1993, September 1993. I personally received in one day 51 bodies. These were civilians who were killed in the Medak pocket. In this Medak pocket, it was the first time that UNPROFOR had an armed conflict with one of the warring parties and that was the Croatian side. And there were casualties on the Croatian side and the UNPROFOR side. On the UNPROFOR side, it was Canadians. In addition to the 51 bodies that I took over, the UNPROFOR people on their own got 18 bodies from houses that were still smouldering, and they handed them over to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us when Operations Flash and Storm took place. Just the dates.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Flash, the 1st and 2nd of May, 1995, and Storm, on 4th of August, that same year, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards all these operations of the Croat forces, what did General Jean Cot say, the UNPROFOR commander whose headquarters were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Actually, he provided a definition in 1993 when he visited the Medak pocket, he said what scorched earth was. So these were scorched earth operations. That means when there is nothing left, no animals, no human beings and when property is destroyed. So Medacki Dzep, the Medak pocket, was carried out according to that principle, and the operations that preceded it and those that followed later. Specifically with regard to Medak pocket, he said that after having visited the terrain for an entire day, three villages and several hamlets, he did not find any human beings or any animals, and he said that the destruction was planned, systematic, and total.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more case, that is, Grubori, and we'll end on that note. What was the participation of UNPROFOR in that case? When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, the 25th of August, UNPROFOR was still there on the ground. There were other UN teams there as well. In addition to their presence, or rather, in spite of their presence, the Croats entered the village of Grubori and carried out cleansing. That's what I'm pointing out. Cleansing. That means that they cleansed Grubori of human beings. They found six or seven old people and they killed them. The UNPROFOR people found them as they were dying, as blood was still seeping from their slit throats, and their houses were still burning. And the Croats said to UNPROFOR that they were fighting the Chetniks still, and these were actually just very old people. In the Gotovina et al case, this was discussed at length, before this Tribunal, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, what you heard about Grubori, any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We wasted another few minutes. No dispute about this matter at all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am glad that we heard that there is no dispute, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if would you have known, if you would have studied the charges brought against some of the accused in that other case that was mentioned, you could have thought that possibly the Prosecution would have no dispute with you about that matter. At least it was worthwhile to explore it. And would you, rather, take my comments seriously than to make the kind of observations as you did last time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened in Grubori? Was it recorded; and if so, who did the recording?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR people had cameras on the ground and they kept recording this, and they sent this footage somewhere and one could see that. I also had an opportunity to see that. Later on, all of this was put together by a person called Bozidar Knezovic who lived in Croatia. I don't know what his ethnicity is. Some people say that he's Montenegrin and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. Do you have any personal knowledge, apart from what you saw on videos, about what happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge comes later with regard to exhumation and identification of bodies from these locations. That is what I deal with, talking to their families, interviewing them, the post-mortems, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simply answer is you don't have any direct observation. You were not asked about exhumations. You were asked about what happened in Grubori and you have no first-hand knowledge of that. That's one. Second, there seems to be not that much dispute about what happened in Grubori. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, with factual questions relevant for us, matters which are not in dispute. I mean matters that are in dispute; I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, thank you for having answered our questions. This is all that the Defence had for you at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. You, indeed, stayed even within the time you claimed. That's appreciated. Mr. Zec, what would you preferably do? To take the break now and then start cross-examination after the break, or would you already start for five, six minutes at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm at your convenience, Your Honours. I can start with some questions, but either way if you feel the break is more appropriate, we can do it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps in order not to interrupt the flow of evidence, we take the break first. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, as some guidance for cross-examination, if the Prosecution considers a certain matter not very relevant, then it's also not that relevant to spend a lot of time on it in cross-examination. Of course, maybe irrelevant matters may raise a need to test credibility and reliability of a witness, but to explore large fields which you consider irrelevant might not be the best way to approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. You'll find him to your right. The same guidance applies; that is, focus on the question. Do not go beyond that. If Mr. Zec wants to know more detail, he'll certainly ask you for it. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You already told us that you worked as a judge in Benkovac, and in 1990 that you had -- that you were defence counsel. In late 1991, you were a member of the Benkovac Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Territorial Defence a lot before that but including 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to focus my question and I'd really appreciate it if you could also focus your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33422.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you have seen this document before, Mr. Strbac. This is a list of the Benkovac TO from September 1991. And we would need to look at item 26. In the English, we need the second page. Item 26, there is "Savo Strbac, Chief of Intelligence." This is you; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33422 receives exhibit number P7637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You were a member of the SAO Krajina commission for exchanges; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: From 1993, you were the secretary of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You served in the RSK government under Milan Martic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: We have to clarify that a bit. Milan Martic was in the government for a while, in the government where I was secretary, Ministry of Interior. So he was not my prime minister; he was just a minister in government. And then in the beginning of 1994, he became president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question, then, was did you work under him? Did you or did you not work under him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is so broad, "under him." He was not my direct superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not work under him. That's the answer. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus to your evidence about the role of the JNA in Croatia. You were aware, were you not, that the JNA was acting as a buffer zone between the conflict parties to a certain moment. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And from a certain moment, the JNA stopped to act as a buffer zone but openly supported the Serb side in the conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And that moment was approximately when General Mladic came to Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, now one has to look at dates, when it was that he arrived and when this happened. I don't know the exact date of his arrival, but I know approximately when the JNA supported one side, stood on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. Perhaps we can call a document, 65 ter 6754, just in terms of efficiency, we can maybe going through faster. This is an interview with Milan Martic from 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have page 10 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So Milan Martic said: "General Mladic came in June or July 1991, managed to create self-confidence to Serbs, and openly stated that Serbs were right. Until that moment JNA and its officers were a buffer zone between us and Croatians ... Mladic openly said ... that the Serbs were right." So this is right, right, that the JNA served as a buffer before General Mladic's arrival and then openly sided with Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Not right. The buffer continued up until September, and I co-operated with people who -- I mean, in addition to the JNA, representatives of the federal SUP were there in the buffer zone. I co-operated with them on a daily basis in Dalmatia, so I knew them. This is what Mladic said. But I'm telling you what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's fine. We're going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, could you tell us to whom this interview was given?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is, Your Honour, an interview with Milan Martic by documentary, "Death of Yugoslavia," so that's when they interviewed Milan Martic, among others, and this is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- all ten pages? Because it's only a small portion which you read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The excerpt is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excerpt is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then you should upload the excerpt, and we reserve a number for it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The excerpt of 65 ter number 06754 receives exhibit number P7638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I want to focus a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is now reserved for an excerpt still to be uploaded. Could we receive that within, let's say, one or two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, now focussing a little bit more on the operations of the units under the command of General Mladic, you were aware that in late 1991 units under the command of General Mladic were engaged in offensive operations in the area of Krajina towards the sea; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some operations towards Sibenik, I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P4909.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an order by General Mladic of 16 September 1991. It is entitled: "Order for Attack - Operational Order Number 1." So in item number 2, it says: "I decided the following: In a co-ordinated action with the Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac TO forces, launch a general attack towards the sea ..." So, first, we see here Benkovac TO. You were aware of this operation because this is your unit, the Benkovac TO; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I said that I knew that then, in September, there were certain operations, and it can also be seen from this first paragraph what the reason was, why this order was issued; that is to say, to de-blockade the barracks and institutions of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you knew about this because the order deals with your unit. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have an answer. That was the question. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm answering for the third time. Yes, there were these operations in September. Now I see what the date is and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was not whether there were operations. The question was whether you knew about this operation because it was your unit that was involved. That's the question. If you don't want to answer it, fine, then we'll move on. But that was the question which you have not answered three times. Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by the answer that I provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which was not an answer to the question. Mr. Zec, you're invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When this order was implemented, the Serb forces led by the JNA attacked areas in the Krajina towards the sea, including the town of Drnis, among others; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question. Now you asked me specifically about Drnis. Well, I don't know. Drnis was far away from Benkovac. I really don't know. Maybe yes; maybe no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, you already said that you know all the operations towards Sibenik so you can confirm that Drnis is located from Knin, towards Sibenik, about halfway through; right? And that's the operation that you were referring to; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: No. I was not referring to Drnis. Drnis is in the hinterland and now I'm talking or I did talk about places along the coast. That's why I'm not sure about Drnis. It depends which route you take from Knin to Sibenik. There's several routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, you can confirm, can you, that Drnis was a Croat majority town. It's about 75 per cent Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I know that the population was mixed, but now I hear what the proportion is. Now I hear it from you. Maybe yes; maybe no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that military operations under the command of General Mladic included forcible removable of non-Serb population from the areas where the 9th Corps was active, and this can be found in P4166, e-court page 42. And then this is what happened to Drnis among other places: Croat populations had to leave Drnis after it was attacked; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that the entire Croat population moved out of Drnis. Now, how many people moved out, you know, after all of these operations, people went in different directions. Some people went towards Bosnia; some people towards Serbia; others, towards Sibenik. I really don't know how many left Drnis then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You know that Drnis became part of the SAO Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see P4913. And this is an interview with General Mladic in late October 1991. It should be P4913. In English, we have a good document but not in the B/C/S. Okay. Can we now have second page in the B/C/S. And if we can zoom to the article which is a bit to the right, the lower part of the page, and the title is "Mladic: Drnis will be called Ratko." So in the second of this article, it says: "Asked when the people of Drnis would return to their homes and what the current situation was in occupied Drnis, Mladic said: 'Drnis used to be a very wild town. It is now tame and it will stay like that.' When a journalist made a comment that Drnis is a Croatian town, Mladic said: 'It was before but never again. Drnis is a part of the SAO Krajina.'" So, this is a reflection of the reality. General Mladic's objective was to ensure that Drnis be part of the SAO Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know how to answer this question of yours. I see this interview for the first time, and I have never heard that Drnis would be called Ratkovo. I guess it's on the basis of his name. But it is a fact that Drnis was in the Republic of the Serb Krajina all the way up until the fall, that is to say, August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's another town that was majority Croat. It was 92 per cent Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ten days after General Mladic ordered attack on Sinj, as we've seen on the order that I showed you, he met Croat represents from Sinj. And we have a video that he went and I'm going to show you a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 33408d and this is an excerpt of a video dated 26 September 1991. Your Honours, the CLSS has kindly checked the accuracy of the translation and we can play it once. The transcripts have been provided. And I also want to note that we will play this clip in two portions. First we will play 1 minute and 26 seconds from the beginning, and then the last 22 seconds. We marked that on the transcripts that have been provided so the Trial Chamber can see what's going to be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, I have the impression that the court reporter would be happy if you would slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Everything movable has to be pulled out. You know that we've already mined all our buildings and installations in all the occupied areas. We are not going for withdrawal. I will open up the road by force. It's not difficult for me. I wouldn't like to do it. You know how I do it. I have to say all this destruction so far does not come even close to what's going to happen if anyone's recklessness or deliberate action infringes upon this. I don't want you to understand this as a threat. I am a soldier. I carry out my tasks. I am a soldier. I carry out my missions. If people had listened to me, there would have been no Kijevo. If people had listened to me, Vrlika would not have happened. If people had listened to me, Hrvace wouldn't have happened. If people had listened to me, Sibenik wouldn't have happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now see the last 22 seconds of this clip. Again, it is marked on the transcript for the translators what will be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any technical problem or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I think it's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] In that case, you can count on having Sinj. In the contrary case you can tell the residents of Sinj and those who are deciding on their fate. "The other man: We won't be conveying that message to them. We will do everything and you will keep that message to yourself. We will do everything. "Mladic: That there will be ... that they can just wait for me in a destroyed city."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, here General Mladic threatened to destroy Sinj if his demands were not met; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this was also his approach to Kijevo, Vrlika, Sibenik, which he says need not have been destroyed if they just listened to him; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Everybody heard this in this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are being asked a question, not being asked whether everybody heard. Please answer the question that is being put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I would now need to ask for the video to be repeated. I think I've heard it well. I didn't hear every word very clearly, but if you did, then that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But upon your recollection where you heard most of it, you agree with Mr. Zec that General Mladic threatened to destroy Sinj if his demands were not met, and that his approach to Kijevo, Vrlika, Sibenik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We take that, then, for agreeing with Mr. Zec that that's what Mr. Mladic said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: General Mladic also sought to fulfil his objectives in these areas by cutting off utilities, such as water, electricity; correct? Right? Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: General Mladic also sought to fulfil his objectives in these areas by cutting off utilities, such as water, electricity, to people like Sinj; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Again, are you asking me again if I had heard it from this video or whether I know it from my experience? You are still asking me what Mladic said in this video. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a man who met Mladic and participated in negotiations with General Mladic. So this was his style. He would even sought to -- he would even cut utilities to people in trying to fulfil his objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I did not hear that, but I know the reverse is true. Barracks had their water supplies, everything cut off, when they were under blockade. I don't know what you're asking. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 33408a. This is another portion of the same event that we've just seen. And, again, Your Honours, thanks to the CLSS we can play it only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive English interpretation at this moment, so could we start again. Transcripts being provided and verified, could we also receive English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I can repeat 65 ter if it is helpful to the translators. It is 33408a.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've got it. Apologies for earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apology accepted. Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] We would need to make arrangements on this and start as soon as possible, because it's in the interest ... I'm not turning anything on, not the water or anything else at all or the bridge or anything else until this ... I won't open the bridge until we also do Dalmatia like this, everything, and I'm not turning your power on. All of this, what I say here, goes also for Dalmatia and beyond, nothing that has been attacked."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is the truth: General Mladic fulfilled his objectives by cutting off utilities; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm things in this way. I know that we were sometimes left without electricity, both sides, very often at that time. Who cut off to whom depends on across whose territory the transmission and supply lines went. I don't know what he means here. I'm answering you to the best of my recollection and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was asking you specifically about General Mladic because you knew General Mladic; you participated in negotiations with him. This is the way he fulfilled his objectives; right? If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would tender these clips and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear whether the witness has an answer to the question. Do you have an answer? Do you not know? Do you not know? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear for the first time what Mladic said at this meeting, and it's silly for me to comment upon what he said at some meeting which I didn't attend. If you are asking me if this happened in practice, I'm telling you that very often we, in Benkovac and Knin and the people in Zadar, were frequently left without electricity. Who cut off power to whom, whether it was caused by shelling that hit some sort of transmission line, I don't know. All I know is that I often suffered blackouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, the answer is that you don't know. Mr. Zec, you tendered this document, this video. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the one before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the one before. They are separate 65 ter numbers. Are they provided on one or on two separate discs? Two discs to be fetched. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may before you continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously, this is a pretty high 65 ter number, and I don't know if we have this one, the complete video. We should see what actually were demands of General Mladic I think, so we need the whole video at least to see it and why he put those requests, so what was the reason, what was the source of these requests. We cannot see it from these clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, first of all, was the clip in its totality disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It was, Your Honours, and I think Mr. Lukic is referring to the portion of the first clip that I played, but we skipped a bit so I think he is referring to that and we have no problem if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must say it caught my attention as well that where it takes even more time to stop it, to restart it, where only 15 seconds, I think, were taken out, I do not know why you took those 15 seconds out, or 20. But if Mr. Lukic would like to have those in, or do you want to have other portions as well, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We really have to go through the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that we admit what is tendered now and that you have an opportunity, well, let's say, this week, to suggest any additions, and then we would finally decide on what the clips are that will be -- that may replace the ones tendered now and admitted now because there is no objection against those portions in itself. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33408d receives exhibit number P7639.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the next one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33408a receives exhibit number P7640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zec, therefore, the failing -- the left-out portion of the first one we looked at, you'll finally include that as well, and Mr. Lukic can make whatever suggestions to add something to further contextualise what you have shown to us. Both are admitted into evidence. That's P7639 and P7640. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, this Chamber has also received evidence of General Mladic threatening to embark on the destruction of Zadar. This is P19459 [sic], page 3. And, in fact, this is exactly what he did. He embarked on the destruction of Zadar; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I cannot just confirm the statements you are making. Yes, there was shelling of Zadar. There were some casualties, just as there was shelling from the other side of my town, Benkovac, also causing casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 31642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Zec, 19459 is given a P number but that's already 19.000. Was it a -- is that a 65 ter number or is it an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Your Honour, I referred to P1959, if that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's the correct number, P1959. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I called up 65 ter 31642, and this is a combat report by General Mladic of 4 October 1991. Can we have page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it says: "... continue with offensive operations towards Zadar." You can see it. It's item 3. It says: "I have decided to continue with offensive operations towards Zadar." It says: "Strike the town of Zadar with direct fire artillery weapons ..." So this destroyed the town, Mr. Strbac; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, I am not illiterate and I am reading this, but all this was intended to get to the units that were being blocked in the city of Zadar. Why don't you read that? That's in the same or the next item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's for Mr. Zec himself to decide what he reads to you. If you say in this context, "I want to add something" or if Mr. Lukic asks you any questions about that, but you don't have to comment on what Mr. Zec read to you. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's true, what's been read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, if we can see a map of Zadar just to get some locations. So this is -- 65 ter 33370.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac, this peninsula that we see on the map, that's the historic part of Zadar; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can zoom to the peninsula, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The national museum is approximately north of the centre of the peninsula. On this map, it is marked as Narodi Muzej; can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I must say I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look centre of the map, just north, if you follow, it should say on the map "Narodi Muzej." It's marked.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Well, if I don't see it here, I know I was in Zadar. I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: No, I can't locate it because I just don't see well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you see "Budska Obala," it's north, and it's a third down where it says "Budska Obala," just a little bit south, it's "Narodi Muzej"; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, the national theatre is approximately in the centre of this peninsula; right? It's not marked, but you can tell us that the national theatre is approximately in the centre.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, the church of Saint Sime is to the right, towards the end of the peninsula. It is marked on the map and it says "Sveti Sime"; can you see that? It has a mark across -- toward the exit of the peninsula. You see it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The Prince Palace is just across that church.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: I see Saint Sime. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Prince Palace, that's across the church Saint Sime; correct? It's not marked but you can confirm, right, it's just across the road?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see now 65 ter 33421, and this is a list of damages in the historical part of Zadar. Page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it says: "Inventory of Damages, damaged facilities and places hit during the bombardment of the historic centre of Zadar from 30th September to 7 October 1991," and there's a list of 79 hits in the historic part of Zadar. For instance, if we can turn to page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Zec, could you tell us what part of the indictment you're dealing with at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We're dealing with acts and conduct of General Mladic during his time in Croatia, which is also what the witness was talking about as to what he was doing this Croatia. So I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was background, I take it, then? That's background information about -- background in relation to the charges brought against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But it also goes to this witness's evidence because his evidence was that he was meeting with General Mladic during these negotiations about exchanges in a way to say that General Mladic was trying to do the good thing in Croatia. Now I'm challenging the basis for his knowledge as to what was happening, what was reality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point. At the same time we are going to a level of detail, I think, which I criticised the Defence for going into; that is, well, this is background information but then you lose yourself in details rather than to strike a fair balance between what is background and may shed some light on the personality of the accused. I see that point really well. But I gave you some guidance at the beginning of the cross-examination that you should avoid to do things which I think this Chamber has made critical comments about when the Defence did it. So details like this street, et cetera, et cetera, it's clear to the Chamber that the Defence very much wants to emphasise what was done to the Serbs in 1991 by the Croats and how they responded to that and what their impact was, and I now see that apparently the Defence -- the Prosecution is doing more or less the opposite, is to say what was done to the Croats by the Serbs included Serb activities under the command of the accused. And what we should try to do is to strike the fair balance between what is background and what is foreground and not to spend too much time and too much detail on what, at least for us is clear, the emphasise of the parties is about. If you have one or more questions, we have another two minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, before we continue, I very much urged the Defence to put factual questions where the witness was very much inclined to tell whatever happened at places where he had never been, most likely on the basis of documentation he had. Now, the witness seems to take that very seriously because any question you ask him now about what happened, his response is "I wasn't there so I can't tell you." At the same time, of course, if that is true, or if he says, "Well, I met Mr. Mladic at that moment," and if you then put to him orders where there's no basis yet established for whether he would have known about these orders to be issued or whether these orders were implemented, the witness is exactly doing, I think, what I advised him to do; that is, to limit himself to factual knowledge. But by insisting on those questions, you may want to do the same as the Defence did, but perhaps that doesn't help. And all of that apparently is at least not the core of the case, that is, the events which happened in the time-frame of this -- the time-frame of the indictment. And I'm saying this to you because if both parties start doing it the way -- and it was criticised when the Defence did it, this is similar criticism, then we can spend here a long time in Court on matters which do not assist. I'm not saying that the act and conducts in previous periods is totally irrelevant, but to ask the witness all kind of things because he once meant Mr. Mladic, of course, might not really give the answers that you would like perhaps to receive and which perhaps would assist the Chamber. I leave it to this at this moment. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to add one point of clarification, Mr. President, and not to suggest that the Prosecution won't take onboard the Court's comments. But in respect of the brief discussion about evidence of acts outside the indictment, there was mention of its possible relevance as background or reflections of personality, I would simply note that more classically such evidence is offered for such matters as motive or intent or modus operandi, and certainly with respect to the latter two, those are appropriate bases for the relevance of the material that was discussed in the course of the cross-examination, we would submit, and just to shed light on both its relevance, its application, and the basis for proffering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said I made a few comments on relevance. I gave a few examples. Background, of course, may also include some of the elements you added, which I certainly did not exclude earlier when I was talking about their relevance. But it's good that the parties think about these matters, and they have time to do that until 9.30 tomorrow morning because we adjourn until Wednesday, the 11th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
